chunks: It is narrated: “A loan is a safeguard for zakat. If you are owed money by a man and its repayment is not readily available to you, then count it from the zakat if you wish. There is no harm in a man buying a believing slave from the zakat of his wealth and then freeing him. If the freed one acquires wealth and dies, then his wealth belongs to the people of zakat, because he was purchased with their wealth. If a man buys his father from the zakat of his wealth and frees him, that is permissible. If a believing man dies and you wish to shroud him from the zakat of your wealth, then give it to his heirs so that they shroud him with it. If he has no heirs, then shroud him and count it from the zakat. If other people give his heirs the price of a shroud, then shroud him yourself and count it from the zakat if you wish. What the people gave them remains for them, to manage their affairs with it. If the deceased had a debt, it is not binding upon his heirs to settle it from what you gave them nor from what the people gave them, because it is not inheritance; rather, it is something that came to his heirs after his death.”

If your wealth is in trade, and the merchandise is sought from you at your capital price, yet you do not sell it seeking thereby additional profit, then its zakat is due upon you when a year has passed over it. But if the merchandise is not sought from you at your capital price, then its zakat is not due upon you. If your wealth is absent from you, then its zakat is not due upon you until your wealth returns to you and a year passes over it while it is in your possession, except when your wealth is owed by a man from whom, whenever you wish to take it, it is made available to you; then zakat is due on it. If its benefit returns to you, its zakat becomes binding upon you. If you sell something and take its price, then stipulate upon the buyer the zakat of a year, or two years, or more, then that is permissible and binding upon him instead of you. If you borrow wealth from a man and it remains with you until a year passes over it, then zakat is due upon you regarding it.

Do not give the zakat of your wealth to other than the people of wilayah, and from among the people of wilayah do not give it to the parents, the child, the husband, the wife, the slave, the grandfather, the grandmother, and everyone whose maintenance a man is compelled to provide. There is no harm, however, in giving zakat to the brother, the sister, the paternal uncle, the paternal aunt, the maternal uncle, and the maternal aunt.

key_terms.كَفَنٍ: the burial shroud of the deceased
key_terms.نَفَقَتِهِ: the maintenance expenses one is legally obligated to provide
key_terms.ٱلتِّجَارَةِ: commercial trade in which wealth is invested
key_terms.ٱلزَّكَاةِ: the obligatory alms due on qualifying wealth
key_terms.ٱلْحَوْلُ: the passing of a full year for zakat liability
key_terms.ٱلْقَرْضَ: a loan or debt connected here to zakat treatment
key_terms.ٱلْوَلَايَةِ: the sphere of loyalty and allegiance that defines eligible recipients here

ai.seo_question: Who may receive zakat, and when is zakat due on debts, trade goods, and borrowed wealth?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out a range of legal rulings concerning zakat, including debts, trade goods, absent wealth, borrowed money, burial shrouds, and the categories of people eligible to receive zakat. It also specifies that zakat should be given within the people of wilayah and not to those whose maintenance is already obligatory upon the giver.
